figure.name: Milton Friedman
figure.role: Economist focused on money, inflation, markets, monetarism, and limits on broad state control.
figure.hook: Friedman = money, inflation, and market liberalism.
whyHere: Friedman belongs here because the page needs the modern market-liberal argument after Keynes and Hayek.
He matters because debates over public spending, inflation, taxation, welfare states, and markets need a clear account of the anti-planning and anti-intervention side.
figure.cleanIdea: Friedman's path argues that money, inflation, incentives, and market freedom matter when judging public policy.

ideas.title: Monetarism
ideas.plainDefinition: Monetarism is an economic view that treats the money supply as central to inflation and economic stability.
ideas.context: In the Friedman path, monetarism is the argument that inflation cannot be understood without money and central-bank policy.
ideas.whyMatters: Monetarism matters because it gives the market-liberal road a specific economic claim instead of a vague dislike of government.

ideas.title: Inflation
ideas.plainDefinition: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, reducing the purchasing power of money.
ideas.context: In the Friedman path, inflation is tied to money, policy choices, and the limits of public spending promises.
ideas.whyMatters: Inflation matters because any honest study of public spending has to ask how programs are funded and what happens to prices.

ideas.title: Market Liberalism
ideas.plainDefinition: Market liberalism emphasizes private exchange, competition, property rights, prices, and limits on state economic control.
ideas.context: In the Friedman path, market liberalism is the modern argument for market coordination and against broad state planning.
ideas.whyMatters: Market liberalism matters because the page needs capitalism's strongest policy defenses, not just socialist critiques of capitalism.
